extracted.intended_audience: creative writers and writing teachers seeking guidance on representing people/cultures other than their own
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and classroom-derived standards for writing characters and cultures different from the writer, focused on respectful representation, research, pedagogy, and use of sensitivity readers. Suitable for workshop leaders and writers across genres wanting practical, ethical craft principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: ROAARS categories
rubrics_metrics.description: ROAARS stands for race, (sexual) orientation, age, ability, religion, and sex — a pronounceable acronym used as a framework for the primary axes of difference to consider when writing others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ROAARS as a starting checklist for which differences matter in representation; recognize that the original list omitted topics (e.g., class) that may now be significant and that the categories should be updated as culture changes (e.g., adding class, cis/trans status, citizenship). The authors note the acronym was chosen for pronounceability and as a pedagogical tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge your own biases and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should explicitly recognize their own biases and privileges before attempting to write people different from themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-awareness is an initial, necessary step toward careful representation; teachers should prompt students to examine assumptions as part of the craft. This is framed as part of fostering humility rather than forbidding attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster diligence and intentionality in representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Respectful portrayals require deliberate effort — diligence and intention — rather than taking an 'easy path' in creative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors emphasize that doing the work well is difficult and requires sustained care; avoid shortcuts that rely on stereotypes or laziness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do research and seek immersive consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should research thoroughly and, when appropriate, immerse or consult people with lived experience relevant to the material they are writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research goes beyond surface facts; it includes talking to, hiring, or otherwise consulting knowledgeable people (cultural consultants) who can help assess accuracy and harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional sensitivity readers / cultural consultants
rubrics_metrics.description: When a writer asks whether a particular premise, passage, or story is harmful, the recommended response is to consult a professional cultural consultant or sensitivity reader rather than rely solely on the instructor's or author's opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity readers can immerse themselves in the work and provide informed feedback; availability and best practice for finding them changes over time, so seek up-to-date resources and professional services rather than ad-hoc judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice actively with exercises and prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Include interactive exercises and prompts so writers can put concepts into practice rather than only read about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book derives from a class and includes exercises used in teaching; doing the work (practice exercises) advances skill more than passive reading. Teachers should incorporate hands-on assignments drawn from workshop practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow mistakes as part of learning; create a safe environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning to write others well requires making mistakes; teachers should cultivate an atmosphere conducive to trying things, learning, and improving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-class practices include a pledge to reinforce group safety and openness, clear guidelines and expectations, and counseling students that mistakes are part of learning. This reduces fear and encourages experimentation while still emphasizing responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply consistent guidelines across online and in-person formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop parameters, expectations, and safety practices should be applied equally in online and in-person classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online students should receive the same preparatory materials and be required to sign the same agreements as in-person participants; instructors should make expectations explicit before the first session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update demographic frameworks over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Frameworks for difference (like ROAARS) should be revised to reflect changing sociocultural realities, adding categories such as class, cis/trans status, and citizenship when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors solicit student updates to category lists in current teaching; being proactive about revisions helps keep instruction inclusive and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid erasure by being specific about identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not subsume distinct identities (e.g., atheism, agnosticism, areligion) under broad labels like 'religion' if that erases meaningful differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in labeling and representation because conflating or erasing groups has cultural and legal consequences; consider how broad categories may mask important distinctions in characters' lived experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prohibit writing other perspectives; teach how to do it responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than telling writers they must not write outside their own identity, instructors should teach methods for doing so thoughtfully and responsibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pedagogical stance is pro-engagement with other perspectives coupled with the tools (research, consultation, humility, practice) to minimize harm. Emphasize learning and improvement over forbiddance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide and recommend further craft resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend and use other craft texts and anthologies that deepen writers' skills in voice, description, outlining, and theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interview lists specific recommended books (e.g., Samuel R. Delany's About Writing; Take Off Your Pants! by Libbie Hawker; Pocket Workshop; Ex Marginalia) as complementary resources for writers seeking to improve structural craft and representation skills.
